questions.stem: Reading the Louisiana Purchase column of a territorial map, a class sees that the 1820 line crossed the remainder of the Purchase and stopped there. Explain which lands the settlement left outside its own rule.

answer.exemplar: The Missouri Compromise line governed the Louisiana Purchase, so the territory of Florida, the Republic of Texas, and later the Mexican cession were untouched by it. The bargain therefore regulated one block of acquired land and left every other acquisition to a later political argument, which is why the question had to be reopened in 1850.

questions.explanation: The rule reached the Louisiana Purchase and no further, so Florida, Texas and later the Mexican cession were not covered. Those lands required new bargains, and 1850 supplied one.
questions.hint: Ask which purchases the 1820 rule never touched.

answer.exemplar: Congress already held complete legislative authority over the District of Columbia, so ending the slave trade there required no new claim of federal power. questions.stem: The District of Columbia row in a table of 1850 legislation separates two ideas, the trade and the holding. Explain why the section on the trade was the part that could be enacted.

answer.exemplar: Ending the trade meant Congress would no longer allow the buying and sale of enslaved people to be carried into the district, and it could do that because Congress governs the district directly. Abolition of slavery already there was a different matter, because owners had a property right and no consent had been given, so the section on holding pledged Congress not to act without the owners' consent.

questions.explanation: The trade was activity Congress could end in a district it governs; the holding of enslaved people already there rested on property rights. The law traded the first for a pledge on the second.
questions.hint: Ask which of the two powers Congress plainly held.

answer.exemplar: The Missouri line of 1820 had been drawn by statute, and repeating that line across the new Mexican cession would have reopened the sectional argument the 1820 bargain had tried to close. questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: Annexation of Texas and its boundary
questions.learningObjective: Identify the two questions the 1849 arrangement settled together
questions.stem: A bond column in a table of the 1849 arrangement shows money issued to Texas and a new western line for the state. Which two things did that arrangement settle together?

options.text: The disputed strip and the slavery status of New Mexico, both by a vote
options.misconception: Believes a popular vote settled both

options.text: The disputed strip and the western boundary of Texas, both without new conquest
The western boundary and the price of the public debt, both paid in gold
options.misconception: Thinks gold payment settled the border

options.text: The strip and the admission of California, both in the same measure
options.misconception: Believes California joined the strip agreement

questions.explanation: The 1849 arrangement delivered the disputed strip to New Mexico and drew Texas's western edge at the 100th meridian, paying Texas through bonds. The border was closed without either side taking new ground.
questions.hint: Ask what the strip's ownership decided and where the line went.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: Annexation by consent
questions.learningObjective: Explain why consent and debt terms were bound together in 1845
questions.stem: A consent column in a table of 1845 lists the approval of the people of Texas and a requirement about the public debt. Explain why those two were bound together.

answer.exemplar: The consent of the people of Texas and the assumption of a portion of Texas's public debt were conditions of the same resolution, and one depended on the other. A legislature of settlers who had spent a decade running their own republic would not consent to join without some assurance that the federal government would recognise part of the obligations it had incurred, so the government offered the bonds and asked for the vote.

questions.explanation: The settlers of Texas had run their own republic and carried its debts, so the government promised to assume a share in exchange for their consent. Consent and money were two sides of one transaction.
questions.hint: Ask what the Texas government had spent and who should pay.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: The 1850 bargain on the trade and on holding
questions.learningObjective: Explain how the difference in jurisdiction shaped the 1850 bargain

stimulus.body: A jurisdiction column in a table of 1850 legislation marks the District of Columbia as the one area where Congress already held complete authority, and the same column marks the territories as areas where the federal government claimed only a limited power, leaving the status of slavery to the settlers.

questions.stem: A jurisdiction column in a table of 1850 legislation distinguishes two kinds of power. How did that difference shape the bargain?

options.text: Congress could bar slavery in the territories after 1850 by a simple vote
options.misconception: Thinks Congress banned slavery in territories

options.text: Congress could do nothing in the district without the consent of the owners
options.misconception: Believes Congress lacked all power in the district

options.text: Congress could end the trade where it ruled outright and had to bargain elsewhere
Congress had the same power in the district as in the territories
options.misconception: Believes the powers were identical

questions.explanation: Clear jurisdiction let Congress end importation in the district without touching slavery, while in territories it could only offer settlers a choice. Each power was used to its limit.
questions.hint: Ask where Congress's authority was already complete.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: Organising acquired territory
questions.learningObjective: Describe the repeated sequence used to admit new states
questions.stem: A procedure table for admitting states shows the same sequence repeated for each new member. Explain the two rules that sequence always followed.

answer.exemplar: Each admission ran through the same two rules: a territory was organised first, with a governor and a legislature that could pass laws but not vote in Congress, and then it entered as a state whose slavery status was fixed by the line, by the new rule of popular sovereignty, or by the bargain of 1850 that allowed California in as free. A free and a slave state entered together whenever the count had drifted.

questions.explanation: The territory stage came first, and the slavery question was settled as part of admission, usually in a pair. That sequence is why organising territory became a running bargain.
questions.hint: Ask what happened before a state and with it.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: What the 1820 settlement left undecided
questions.learningObjective: Analyse what the settlement closed and what it left open
questions.stem: A blank row in a table of 1820 measures carries a note that the question would be settled by those who lived there. What did that note close, and what did it leave open?

options.text: It closed the admission of new states and left the territories open
options.misconception: Believes new states could not be admitted

options.text: It closed slavery everywhere and left the count of states to be decided
options.misconception: Believes the line ended slavery everywhere

options.text: It closed the question of congressional power and left the line undrawn
options.misconception: Believes the line was never drawn

options.text: It closed the northern line and left the status of new lands to local choice

questions.explanation: The bargain made the north of the line safe and handed the rest to the settlers, closing one question and leaving the great body of new land unsettled. That leftover is what popular sovereignty later filled.
questions.hint: Ask what the note decided and where it pointed.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: The problem a dividing line creates
questions.learningObjective: Explain how an unwritten understanding shaped the 1820 settlement

stimulus.body: A membership table in a newspaper lists the senators of the state that had entered as free in 1820 and shows them sitting in the same chamber as the senators of the new slave state, with two seats each. The caption notes that the arrangement was not written into any statute.

questions.stem: A membership table in a newspaper shows two seats for a free and a slave state. What did the table's caption reveal about how the system worked?

options.text: The balance was set by a statute that both states had ratified together
options.misconception: Believes the pairing was written into law

options.text: The balance was an unwritten understanding, dependent on each new admission
The balance came from an equal apportionment of population in both states
options.misconception: Believes the two states had equal populations

options.text: The balance was maintained by a permanent board of territorial commissioners
options.misconception: Thinks commissioners enforced the balance

questions.explanation: Because the pairing rested on custom rather than statute, it lasted only while each admission was agreed. The first time one state entered alone, the understanding failed at once.
questions.hint: Ask what the caption said about any statute.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: The power the 1820 law claimed for Congress
questions.learningObjective: Identify the central refusal of the 1820 law
questions.stem: A summary table of 1820 legal claims lists the government's position on territorial slavery. What did the 1820 law refuse to do?

options.text: To fix a limit on slavery in the state of Missouri itself
options.misconception: Believes the law left Missouri entirely alone

options.text: To admit Missouri without a condition attached to the admission
options.misconception: Believes Missouri entered without conditions

options.text: To bar slavery in the territories, on the stated ground that it had no such power
To leave the question of a new state's status to its own settlers
options.misconception: Believes the law left status to settlers

questions.explanation: The law claimed Congress could not bar slavery in territories and acted on that claim by letting settlers decide. Yet it still wrote conditions into Missouri's admission, the tension at the heart of the bargain.
questions.hint: Ask what the law said it could not do, and why.
